meta.title: Cholo Puran Dhaka — places dataset
notes: Facts come from the sources listed on each place. Nothing has been checked on site yet.
pin: 'source' means the coordinate came from a published source (mostly Wikipedia). pin: 'approx' means it was placed by street or neighbourhood and must be confirmed standing at the entrance.
quiet and peak times are estimates from sources and general patterns, not observations.
Fees and hours change. Every card should show the research date until a field check replaces it.

places.tagline: The Nawabs' pink palace on the Buriganga
places.whyGo: The one place everyone should see first. The palace of the Dhaka Nawabs is now a museum of their rooms, furniture and portraits, and the riverside staircase is the best-known view in Old Dhaka.
places.history: Built 1859–1872 for Khwaja Abdul Ghani, with Martin & Co. as contractor. A tornado in 1888 wrecked everything except the Rangmahal, and the 1897 earthquake damaged it again. The government restored it from 1985 and it opened as a branch of the Bangladesh National Museum in 1992. The lotus-bud dome rises about 27 m.
closed: Eid day and the day before
places.ticketing: Same-day online tickets at ahsanmanzilticket.gov.bd (4% charge, limited quota) or at the gate.

photo.tips: Shoot the south façade and staircase from the river side, or from a boat on the Buriganga late in the day when the pink warms up.

access.note: Car traffic on Islampur Road is slow; a rickshaw from Sadarghat or Bahadur Shah Park is often quicker.

places.tagline: A Mughal fort that was never finished
places.whyGo: Big lawns, red-brick gateways, and the tomb of Pari Bibi at the centre. It is the calmest large open space in Old Dhaka, which makes it a good stop between crowded lanes.
places.history: Begun in 1678 by Prince Muhammad Azam, son of Aurangzeb, and continued by Shaista Khan. Work stopped after his daughter Pari Bibi died in 1684. Inside are the Diwan-i-Aam with its hammam, a three-domed mosque, the tomb and a square water tank. It was called Fort Aurangabad and renamed Lalbagh Fort in 1844.
places.hours: Oct–Mar: Sat, Tue–Thu 9:00–17:00; Mon 13:30–17:00; Fri 9:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00. Summer hours start an hour later.
places.ticketing: Ticket at the gate. Fees were not published in the sources checked — confirm on site.

photo.tips: Pari Bibi's tomb framed through the south gateway, and its reflection in the water tank on a still evening.

access.note: Mostly flat lawns and paths.

places.tagline: Covered in broken china and blue stars
places.whyGo: Every surface is chinitikri, mosaic made from broken Japanese and English china, with blue stars over the domes. It is small, so you can see all of it in twenty minutes, and the detail rewards standing close.
places.history: Built by Mirza Ghulam Pir (died 1860); sources disagree on whether it dates from the late 18th or early 19th century. Ali Jan Bepari added the star decoration in the early 20th century, and two domes were added in 1987, making five. It appears on the ৳100 note.

photo.tips: Close-ups of the mosaic on the pillars and mihrabs; the courtyard gives a straight-on view of all five domes.
photo.inside: Ask permission and avoid prayer times

access.note: Dress modestly; women should carry a scarf. Remove shoes before entering the prayer hall.

name.en: Armenian Church of the Holy Resurrection

places.tagline: Dhaka's Armenian past, behind a quiet gate
places.whyGo: A white 1781 church in a walled graveyard, two minutes from the noise of Armanitola. Read the old Armenian gravestones; one has a statue of the man's wife.
places.history: Built in 1781 on an Armenian burial ground. Its clock tower lost its clock in 1880 and fell in the 1897 earthquake. About 350 people are buried here. Mother Teresa stayed in the compound in 1996. It is a protected heritage site.
places.hours: Daytime visits; ring at the gate.

photo.tips: The church front from the far side of the graveyard, with the gravestones in the foreground.

access.note: On Armenian Street. Be respectful; it is a working church and a graveyard.

places.tagline: The goddess the city may be named after
places.whyGo: Bangladesh's largest Hindu temple and Dhaka's biggest Durga Puja. Outside festival days it is peaceful, with red-ochre temple towers around a courtyard.
places.history: Traditionally dated to the 12th century and credited to Ballal Sen of the Sena dynasty, though repeated rebuilding means the present structures are later. The original idol went to Kolkata at Partition; a replica is worshipped here. Renamed the National Temple in 1996.

photo.tips: The temple towers across the courtyard in morning light; during Puja, the evening arati.
photo.inside: No photos of the deity without permission

access.note: Remove shoes where asked.

places.tagline: Where Old Dhaka marks Muharram
places.whyGo: A white Shia imambara with a large pond in front. In the first ten days of Muharram it becomes the centre of Old Dhaka's mourning gatherings, ending with the Ashura procession.
places.history: Traditionally founded in 1606–07 by Mir Murad with support from Prince Shah Shuja; the present building is attributed to a 1823 rebuilding by Naib Nazim Nusrat Jung. The flat roof was rebuilt after the 1897 earthquake.

photo.tips: The façade reflected in the pond, shot from the south bank.
photo.inside: Ask first; be discreet during gatherings

access.note: During Muharram, expect crowds and security checks.

places.tagline: A Mughal caravanserai, slowly disappearing
places.whyGo: What is left of a 1640s travellers' inn for merchants. Less than half survives, hemmed in by shops and new building, so see the southern gateway while you still can.
places.history: Built 1644–1646 by Mir Abul Qasim, diwan of Prince Shah Shuja. Its south wing ran about 68 m along the river with a three-storey gateway. Part was demolished in 2022; ownership disputes have kept the Department of Archaeology out.
quiet: Early morning before the shops open
places.hours: Visible from the street; the interior is privately occupied.

photo.tips: The arched gateway from the lane to its south; go early before handcarts block the view.

access.note: Narrow, busy lanes. Be polite with residents and shopkeepers.

places.tagline: Shaista Khan's smaller inn, lost among shops
places.whyGo: Bara Katra's younger sibling, 185 m to the east. Only fragments of the gateways show between shopfronts, so it is a find for people who like hunting for history.
places.history: Built 1663–1671 by Subahdar Shaista Khan. Restoration attempts have not succeeded, and the tomb of Champa Bibi inside is now hidden among shops.

photo.tips: Look up: the old arches sit above modern shop signs.

access.note: Combine with Bara Katra on one walk.

places.tagline: A Mughal mosque raised on its own platform
places.whyGo: Climb the steps to a three-domed mosque standing on a platform about 5 m high, with vaulted rooms underneath. Few visitors come, though it is a short walk from Lalbagh Fort.
places.history: Built around 1704–1706 by Khan Mohammad Mridha under Qadi Ibadullah. The platform holds vaulted rooms (tahkhana); the site also had a madrasa.
quiet: Most of the day outside prayer times

photo.tips: Shoot up the staircase to the domes; the platform gives a view over the lane roofs.

access.note: Steep steps up to the platform.

places.tagline: Dhaka's oldest surviving mosque, from 1454
places.whyGo: A small single-domed mosque older than the Mughals in Dhaka. It is being expanded, so the original building may not look the same for long.
places.history: Built in 1454 by Bakht Binat, daughter of Marhamat, in the reign of Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah. A renovation plan adds a 70-foot minaret and more storeys, and part of the old structure is being demolished.

photo.tips: Find the original single-dome section and frame it apart from the new construction.

access.note: Beside Hayat Bepari's Bridge in Narinda.

places.tagline: The red town hall on the riverbank
places.whyGo: A red Indo-Saracenic town hall from 1880, freshly restored. The outside is the reason to come; good for photos with the river behind you.
places.history: Funded in 1874 and inaugurated in 1880 as Dhaka's town hall. Later used as a telegraph office and a women's college. Restoration by Dhaka South City Corporation began in 2023 and was largely complete by May 2026, with a library planned in Johnson Hall.
places.hours: Exterior visible any time. Interior access was not confirmed as of May 2026.
places.ticketing: Check current opening with Dhaka South City Corporation.

photo.tips: Late-afternoon light on the red façade; include a domed corner tower.

access.note: On Farashganj Road; traffic is heavy.

places.tagline: Ahsan Manzil's old rival, now a spice market
places.whyGo: A riverside mansion with a grand columned portico, once Ahsan Manzil's rival for parties and music. Today spice and vegetable traders work in its halls. It is crumbling, crowded and fascinating.
places.history: Built in 1825 by Armenian merchant Stephen Aratoon, later bought by Ruplal and Raghunath Das and rebuilt by Martin & Co. Ruplal Das hosted a ball for Viceroy Lord Dufferin in 1886. The 1897 earthquake damaged its watchtower. It is protected but badly deteriorated.
places.hours: Occupied by traders and residents; outside view any time.
places.ticketing: No ticket. Parts are private; ask before entering courtyards.

photo.tips: The fluted columns of the portico, and the long façade seen from a boat on the river.

access.note: Beside Buckland Bund. Watch your footing near the market.

places.tagline: Where the Awami League was founded in 1949
places.whyGo: A pastel late-19th-century mansion with a garden and fountain. The state bought it in 2018 to turn it into a museum; check access before you go.
places.history: Built by zamindar Hrishikesh Das to rival nearby Baldha Garden. The Awami League was formed here on 23 June 1949. The government bought it for Tk 331.70 crore in 2018 with plans for a museum.

photo.tips: The façade and fountain from the garden axis.

access.note: In Tikatuli, east of Wari.

places.tagline: A small park with a big 1857 story
places.whyGo: A green pause between Sadarghat and the lanes, with a memorial to the sepoys hanged here in 1857. Refurbished in 2020 with a walking loop, benches and toilets.
places.history: Once the Armenian club ground 'Antaghar'. Sepoys were hanged here during the 1857 uprising, and Queen Victoria's rule was proclaimed here in 1858 (Victoria Park). Renamed after the last Mughal emperor in 1957.

photo.tips: The sepoy memorial with the star-shaped fountain in front.

access.note: Good meeting point; Jagannath University is next door.

places.tagline: The country's first private school, founded 1848
places.whyGo: An Armenian merchant's school that Vivekananda and Michael Madhusudan Dutta visited. Look at it from Chittaranjan Avenue on your way to Bahadur Shah Park.
places.history: Founded 12 June 1848 by Nicholas Pogose, who was also its first headmaster. Moved to Chittaranjan Avenue after 1896 and joined Jagannath University in 2015.
places.hours: A working school; view from outside.

photo.tips: Street view only; don't photograph students.

access.note: 6 Chittaranjan Avenue.

places.tagline: Where Guru Tegh Bahadur stayed in the 1660s
places.whyGo: A two-storey Sikh shrine on the same lane as Beauty Boarding, linked to the ninth Sikh Guru's stay in Dhaka (1666–68). Few people in Dhaka know it exists.
places.history: The original building is gone; the present one has a round balcony and an upstairs prayer room with paintings of Guru Tegh Bahadur. Volunteers from Gurdwara Nanak Shahi hold a morning prayer daily and kirtan on Saturdays.
places.hours: Ask at the door; morning prayer daily.

photo.tips: The round balcony from across the lane.

access.note: 14 Sreesh Das Lane, Banglabazar.

places.tagline: Shaista Khan's 1676 mosque on the market square
places.whyGo: The three-domed mosque at the heart of Chawkbazar. It anchors any walk through the market, and during Ramadan the iftar bazaar spreads out around it.
places.history: Built in 1676 by Subahdar Shaista Khan beside the Mughal market square; about 94 × 80 feet with three domes.

photo.tips: The domes above the market crowd from a nearby rooftop or upper floor, if a shopkeeper lets you up.

access.note: Chawkbazar lanes are packed; keep valuables close.

places.tagline: A zamindar's 1909 botanical garden
places.whyGo: 672 plant species packed into a walled garden in Wari, with old glasshouses and a pond. Quiet, shaded, and a real break from the traffic outside.
places.history: Created from 1909 by Narendra Narayan Roy Chaudhury, landlord of the Balda estate, who kept adding to it until his death in 1943.
places.hours: Open all year; hours not published in sources checked.
places.ticketing: Ticket at the gate. Visitors reported a fivefold fee increase in July 2024 — check the current price.

photo.tips: Macro shots of rare plants; the lily pond in soft morning light.

access.note: In Wari, a short rickshaw ride from Narinda.

places.tagline: Colonial tombs under old trees
places.whyGo: Dhaka's old Christian burial ground, with domed and obelisk tombs from the colonial era. Shaded and silent; walk slowly and read the stones.
places.history: Details not yet researched from a reliable source; to be added after a site visit.
places.hours: Ask the caretaker at the gate.

photo.tips: Side light through the trees on the domed tombs, late afternoon.

access.note: Go in daylight and preferably not alone.

sources.label: Listed for field research; no verified source yet

places.tagline: The country's busiest passenger river port
places.whyGo: Triple-decked launches, vendors leaping between boats, and men praying on deck at sunset. Loud, chaotic and unlike anywhere else in Dhaka.
places.history: A river port since Mughal times; Buckland Bund, the 1864 embankment promenade, ran along this waterfront. Overnight launches to Barishal and the south, such as Sundarban-12, Parabat-18 and Surovi-7, leave in the evening, roughly 18:00–20:00. Since the Padma Bridge opened in 2022 the fleet has shrunk from 90 launches on 42 routes to 62 on 36 (TBS, March 2025).
peak: Early morning and evening, when launches arrive and depart
places.ticketing: Pay the small entry fee at the gate. Overnight cabins to Barishal cost about Tk 1,000–2,000 and sell out; book through an agency or arrive by 17:00.

photo.tips: Sunrise or the hour before sunset, from a pontoon or a small boat looking back at the launches.
photo.inside: Open air; ask before photographing people up close

access.note: Busy, noisy and dirty. Watch your pockets and your step on pontoons.

sources.label: Away with the Steiners: Dhaka to Barisal by launch

places.tagline: See Old Dhaka from the water
places.whyGo: Hire a small wooden boat with one oarsman by the hour, from beside the terminal. From mid-river, Ahsan Manzil, Ruplal House and the launches line up in one view.
places.history: Old Dhaka was once called the 'Venice of the East' for its river trade.
places.ticketing: Agree the price per hour before you get in; rates are rising as more tourists come.

photo.tips: Late afternoon: the light falls on the Old Dhaka bank.

access.note: Boats are small and low. Not ideal for elders or small children; no life jackets are usually provided.

places.tagline: The conch-bangle lane
places.whyGo: A narrow street of 12-foot-wide, very deep houses, small shrines, and shops cutting conch-shell bangles. During Durga Puja it is lit up end to end; on normal days it is quieter and worn.
places.history: Named after the Shankhari community of conch-shell artisans. The 1971 massacre here devastated the community. Houses are about 12 ft wide and 70–100 ft deep, each traditionally with a shrine room.

photo.tips: Look straight down the lane to compress the narrow façades; at Puja, the lights after dark.
photo.inside: Ask before photographing inside homes or shrines

access.note: Near Islampur Road and Nawabpur Road, one block north of the river.

sources.label: The Daily Star: Shankhari Bazar at Durga Puja

places.tagline: Kite makers before Shakrain
places.whyGo: In the weeks before Shakrain, the kite makers here and in Shankhari Bazar are busy with paper kites and spools of string. Come in early January to see it.
places.history: One of the old artisan quarters next to Shankhari Bazar.

photo.tips: Stacks of kites in shopfronts; hands working string.

access.note: Walk it together with Shankhari Bazar.

places.tagline: Bolts of colour behind Ahsan Manzil
places.whyGo: A wholesale cloth district of fabric shops stacked floor to ceiling. Walk it on the way to or from Ahsan Manzil.
places.history: One of Old Dhaka's main wholesale textile streets.

photo.tips: Shopfronts of stacked fabric; look for colour, not faces.

access.note: Porters carry heavy loads; step aside for them.

places.tagline: Ramadan's most famous food street
places.whyGo: Every Ramadan afternoon the square fills with stalls: shahi jilapi, keema paratha, koel roast and the legendary 'boro baper polay khay'. Go for the spectacle, even if the food doesn't always match the hype.
places.history: Chawkbazar has been the old city's market square since Mughal times; Subahdar Shaista Khan built the Chawk Mosque beside it in 1676, and the Naib Nazim Mirza Lutfullah rebuilt the bazaar in 1728.

photo.tips: The giant jilapi coils and the crowd under stall lights.

access.note: Roads close to vehicles at peak hours. Extremely crowded; not for elders or small children.

sources.label: Asia News Network: Is Dhakaiya food worth the hype?

places.tagline: The book publishing heart of the country
places.whyGo: Nearly 200 publishers and thousands of bookshops in narrow lanes, with porters carrying fresh books on their heads. Busiest in the weeks before the Ekushey Book Fair.
places.history: Bookshops appeared after 1857. Buddhadeb Basu's first poetry book was published here in 1925, and after 1947 it became the base of East Pakistan's publishers.
peak: December–January, before the February book fair

photo.tips: Porters with book stacks; printing presses through open doors.

access.note: Combine with Beauty Boarding and Cafe Corner.

sources.label: The Daily Star: Banglabazar, all things book

places.tagline: Where Bangladesh's poets drank their evening tea
places.whyGo: A plain Bengali lunch in a courtyard where Shamsur Rahman, Al Mahmud and Syed Shamsul Huq once gathered. Come for the history and the room, not a fancy meal.
places.history: The building housed the Shonar Bangla newspaper before 1947. A restaurant and boarding house opened here around 1951 and became a meeting place for writers and artists.
places.hours: Lunch and tea hours; not published.

photo.tips: The courtyard and the old signboard.

access.note: 1 Sreesh Das Lane, Banglabazar. Basic facilities.

sources.label: Moha-Mushkil: best food in Puran Dhaka

places.tagline: Mutton crumb chop and tea in white cups
places.whyGo: A tiny non-AC snack room across the road from Beauty Boarding. Order the mutton crumb chop and milk tea.

photo.tips: Tea service on the marble tables.

access.note: Seats about 20–25.

sources.label: Moha-Mushkil: best food in Puran Dhaka

places.tagline: Goat biryani on a leaf, since 1939
places.whyGo: Haji Mohammad Hossain's goat (chevon) biryani, cooked with mustard oil and served on a jackfruit-leaf plate with borhani. The original shop on Kazi Alauddin Road is the one to go to.
places.history: Started in 1939 as a roadside food corner with one pot; the family still runs it.

photo.tips: The big pot being opened, and the leaf plate.

access.note: 70 Kazi Alauddin Road, Nazira Bazar. Many shops copy the name; the original says it has few branches.

sources.label: S M Shahinul Islam: Biryani scene of Dhaka

places.tagline: Morog polao from Baburchi Nanna Mia's kitchen
places.whyGo: The original Nanna Mia shop for morog polao (chicken pulao), biryani, rezala, firni and borhani. Look for the Becharam Dewri address; the name is copied all over the city.
places.history: Started by Baburchi Nanna Mia in the 1960s; the family still runs it.

photo.tips: The polao being served from the degchi.

access.note: 41 Becharam Dewri, Moulvibazar area. Copycat shops use the same name.

sources.label: S M Shahinul Islam: Biryani scene of Dhaka

places.tagline: Lassi and lemon sherbet since 1922
places.whyGo: Order the lebu sherbet: gondhoraj lemon with the slice rubbed on the rim. The lassi is made with sweet curd, and the falooda is heavy and generous. A short menu done well for a century.
places.history: Founded by Abdul Aziz on 15 June 1922; the original shop is at 30/1 Johnson Road, with branches in Nazira Bazar and elsewhere. Falooda was added in 2000.
places.ticketing: Falooda was Tk 100 in one recent review.

photo.tips: The glasses lined up on the counter.

access.note: 30/1 Johnson Road. Small; you may stand.

sources.label: Moha-Mushkil: best food in Puran Dhaka

places.tagline: Rows of bhorta and a cheap, honest lunch
places.whyGo: A long-time student favourite for a spread of bhortas, ilish, shutki and curries at low prices. Go hungry and point at the bowls.
places.history: Near the old Central Jail on Nazimuddin Road; popular with Dhaka University and BUET students for decades.

photo.tips: The bhorta bowls laid out at the counter.

access.note: Nazimuddin Road.

sources.label: The Daily Star: Dhaka's food joints

places.tagline: Mutton chaap off the coals at night
places.whyGo: Known for mutton chaap and beef gurda (kidney) kebab, best after dark when Nazira Bazar turns into a late-night food street.

photo.tips: Smoke and flame at the grill; shoot from the side, not over the cook.

access.note: Vehicles can't enter Nazira Bazar lanes at night.

places.tagline: Kacchi, morog polao and mutton 'glassy'
places.whyGo: A big, busy Old Dhaka restaurant for kacchi biryani, morog polao and the mutton 'glassy'. Good when you want a sit-down meal with family.

photo.tips: Plates at the table.

access.note: Bangshal area.

places.tagline: Nolli biryani, gone by four
places.whyGo: Famous for nolli (bone-marrow) biryani. It is a daytime shop, so go before lunch ends.
places.history: Founded by Abdul Kader Mia in 1950 and continued by his son Hazi Makhon.

photo.tips: The marrow bone on the plate.

access.note: Nasir Uddin Sardar Lane, Raisaheb Bazar.

sources.label: S M Shahinul Islam: Biryani scene of Dhaka

places.tagline: A breakfast biryani that sells out by nine
places.whyGo: A morning-only biryani with light spicing, in the lane opposite the Shahi Mosque. Chicken pulao on Mondays and Wednesdays. Arrive early or miss it.
places.history: Running since the 1960s.
places.hours: Mornings only, usually sold out by 9:00.

photo.tips: Morning light in the lane.

access.note: In the Banik Samiti lane, opposite Chawkbazar Shahi Mosque.

sources.label: S M Shahinul Islam: Biryani scene of Dhaka

places.tagline: Tokens at 3 am, sold out before dawn
places.whyGo: A pulao sold in the middle of the night from a stall with no proper shop. Tokens go out from about 3 am and when they run out, you go home hungry. For the committed only.
places.history: Started by Manik Chan's father about 70 years ago.

photo.tips: The queue under a single bulb.

access.note: Dighubabu Lane — ask locally; the pin is a rough guess. Go with friends at that hour.

sources.label: S M Shahinul Islam: Biryani scene of Dhaka

places.tagline: Flaky bread from clay ovens
places.whyGo: Watch bakarkhani slapped onto the walls of clay tandoors and buy it warm: sweet, salty, butter-fried or cheese. Old Dhaka's classic breakfast with tea.
places.history: A Mughal-era bread kept alive in Old Dhaka, especially in Lalbagh, Chankharpul, Nazimuddin Road and Agamasi Lane.
places.ticketing: About Tk 110–120 per kg in 2019; check current prices.

photo.tips: The baker's arm reaching into the tandoor, and stacks of fresh bread.

access.note: Several roadside shops along the lane.

sources.label: TBS: Still in love with Bakarkhani
BSS: Bakarkhani still reigns as Old Dhaka's timeless delight (May 2026)

places.tagline: Rooftops full of kites every January
places.whyGo: On Poush Sankranti in mid-January, Old Dhaka's rooftops fill with families flying and fighting kites. After dark the rooftops get loud with music.
places.history: In 2026 some groups protested the festival, and police banned paper lanterns and fireworks over fire risk and limited sound systems. Check the year's rules before you go.
places.ticketing: Rooftops are private; go with someone who lives here.

photo.tips: Kites against the late-afternoon sky from a rooftop.

access.note: Roofs can have low or no railings; watch children.

places.tagline: A Mughal palace across the river, almost forgotten
places.whyGo: Across the Buriganga from Bara Katra, the remains of a late-17th-century palace hide among houses: seven rooms, two octagonal towers and a broken south gateway. Go for the story and the river crossing, not for polish.
places.history: Built in the late 17th century by Ibrahim Khan II, Bengal's last subedar before Azim-ush-Shan. Legend says a wooden bridge linked it to Bara Katra and a tunnel ran under the river to Lalbagh Fort. What survives is in very poor condition, and locals call it a haveli.
places.hours: Not a managed site; surrounded by private houses.
places.ticketing: No ticket. Ask locals for directions; it is tucked between buildings.

photo.tips: The octagonal towers from the lane, and Old Dhaka's skyline from the boat on the way over.

access.note: On the Keraniganj side. Cross by nouka from the Old Dhaka bank, or by road over Babu Bazar Bridge, then ask for Jinjira Palace. Route details not yet field-checked.

places.tagline: Dhaka's sweet shop since 1864
places.whyGo: The original Chawkbazar shop of a sweetmaker family from Lucknow. Small, with a hand-run counter and a few seats. Come for shar malai, irani bhog and malai bhog, or pick up a box of mixed sweets to share.
places.history: Alauddin Halwai came from Lucknow and opened in Chawkbazar in the 1860s. A Daily Star look back at old Dacca's eateries places 'Alauddin Haluwai' beside Chawkbazar's old hotels, selling puri, jilapi and halwa. The firm now has several outlets, but Chawkbazar is the oldest.

dishes.en: Shar malai, irani bhog, malai bhog
dishes.bn: সর মালাই, ইরানি ভোগ, মালাই ভোগ

photo.tips: The old counter and the trays of sweets behind the glass.
photo.inside: Ask first; it is a working shop

access.note: In the Chawkbazar lanes; there are several branches, so look for the Chawkbazar one.

sources.label: The Business Standard: Alauddin Sweets, a story that began in 1864 (Dec 2020)
The Business Standard: Guilty pleasures of Alauddin Sweetmeat (Nov 2019)
The Daily Star: Eateries of Dacca (Aug 2013)

places.tagline: Nihari for breakfast, gone by eight
places.whyGo: Slow-cooked shank nihari with bone marrow, eaten hot with butter naan or tandoor roti. The cook works through the night, the pot opens at seven, and it usually sells out within the hour. Haleem takes over in the evening.
places.history: Nihari was traditionally a breakfast dish, and this is one of the few places in Dhaka that still serves it that way. The owners say Old Dhaka's nihari was once cooked with nut oils.
places.hours: Daily from 7:00 until the nihari sells out (often by 8:00). Haleem in the evening. Friday special from 10:00.

photo.tips: Steam off the bowls in the early light.

access.note: Subal Das Road, Lalbagh. Arrive by 7:00; on Fridays it is busier and they cook extra.

sources.label: The Business Standard: 5 restaurants around Dhaka for nihari (Nov 2022)
The Daily Star: Why Old Dhaka's Siddiqui Bhai nihari is a must-try (Aug 2025)

places.tagline: Thick nolli nihari on Rankin Street
places.whyGo: A small, cosy room in Wari known for nolli gosht nihari with a thicker gravy than most, and soft, spongy naan. Expect to wait for a table in the evening; takeaway is quicker.
places.history: The Business Standard calls Wari 'old Dhaka's aristocratic lane', and Rankin Street is one of its old roads.
places.hours: Not published; busiest in the evening.

photo.tips: The nihari bowl with the marrow bone.

access.note: Rankin Street, Wari. Dine in or take away.

sources.label: The Business Standard: 5 restaurants around Dhaka for nihari (Nov 2022)

places.tagline: Malai tea, any hour of the day or night
places.whyGo: A tea stall on Kazi Alauddin Road that never closes. Order the creamy malai tea, a plain liquor tea, or the 'Pannu special'. It is the natural stop between biryani and kebabs in Nazira Bazar.
places.history: The family ran a tea stall in New Market from 2008 and opened this store, the first full tea shop on the road, around 2016.

photo.tips: The tea being pulled and poured at the counter.
photo.inside: Fine, it is open to the street

access.note: 37/2 Kazi Alauddin Road, Nazira Bazar.

sources.label: The Business Standard: A precious little tea store (Oct 2019)

places.tagline: Chaap with three kinds of naan
places.whyGo: Known for chaap (flattened, spiced and fried meat) eaten with naan. The signature is chicken vegetable chaap with three kinds of naan. A good dinner stop on a Nazira Bazar food walk.
places.history: Nazira Bazar takes its name from the Mughal-era officials called nazir who lived here.

dishes.en: Chicken vegetable chaap with three naans

photo.tips: The chaap on the tawa.

access.note: In the Nazira Bazar lanes near Kazi Alauddin Road.

places.tagline: Old Dhaka's food street, open at all hours
places.whyGo: Stalls line both sides of Kazi Alauddin Road around the Nazira Bazar crossing: biryani, chaap, kebab, fried beef belly, sweets and bakarkhani. In the morning, look for mattha and chhena; at night, try a fire paan on Agasadek Road.
places.history: The neighbourhood is named after the Mughal-era nazirs. In 1954 Sheikh Fazilatunnesa Mujib moved into a house here after Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's arrest.
places.hours: Stalls are open at almost all hours.

photo.tips: After dark, from the crossing, with the grill smoke and shop lights.
photo.inside: Street; ask before close-ups of people

access.note: Vehicles can't get through at night. It is a walk from Bangabazar, near Gulistan. Keep valuables close in the crowd.

places.tagline: Luchi, bhaji and bhundia for breakfast
places.whyGo: A Lalbagh sweet shop whose breakfast has drawn crowds for about fifty years: deep-fried luchi with mixed vegetable bhaji, and bhundia (gram-flour pearls in syrup) to finish.
places.history: Old Dhaka's sweet shops double as breakfast places, a tradition that goes back generations.

photo.tips: Luchi puffing up in the kadai.

access.note: In Lalbagh; combine with an early visit to the fort.

sources.label: The Daily Star: Feasting on Fridays, Dhaka's breakfast traditions (Sep 2025)

places.tagline: A Mughal mosque with Bengal's only baoli
places.whyGo: A five-domed Mughal mosque raised on a platform with shops underneath, in the middle of Begum Bazar. Look for the baoli, a stepped well to the east, described as the only one of its kind in Bengal.
places.history: Built between 1700 and 1704 by Murshid Quli Khan, then Dhaka's diwan, also known as Kartalab Khan. Mirza Golam Pir renovated it extensively in the 19th century. Locals also call it the Begum Bazar Mosque.

photo.tips: The domes and corner kiosks from the platform; the stepped well from above.
photo.inside: Ask permission and avoid prayer times

access.note: An active mosque. Dress modestly; women should carry a scarf. Remove shoes before the prayer hall.

places.tagline: A white Gothic church from 1821
places.whyGo: A white-plastered Gothic church with a square clock tower, a short walk north of Bahadur Shah Park. Inside: teak furnishings, a stone font and old memorial tablets.
places.history: Built from 1819 to 1821 and consecrated in 1824. It became a cathedral in 1951 and is now the seat of the Church of Bangladesh's Diocese of Dhaka. It was renovated in 2005.
places.hours: Not published; ask at the gate.

photo.tips: The clock tower from Johnson Road.
photo.inside: Ask first; don't photograph during services

access.note: An active church. Combine with Bahadur Shah Park and Pogose School.

places.tagline: The last gateway of the Naib Nazims' palace
places.whyGo: The surviving gate of the 18th-century Nimtali Palace, restored and opened in 2019 as a small museum of Dhaka's 18th and 19th centuries: a recreated Naib Nazim's court, porcelain, coins, paintings and muslin.
places.history: The Naib Nazims, Dhaka's deputy governors, built the palace around 1765–66. The office was abolished in 1843 and the palace fell to ruin. The Asiatic Society, founded on the grounds in 1953, restored the gate in 2009–11.
places.hours: Not published; check with the Asiatic Society before you go.

photo.tips: The restored gate from the courtyard.

access.note: 5 Old Secretariat Road, Nimtali, on the northern edge of Old Dhaka near Chankharpul.

sources.label: The Business Standard: How the Nimtali Deuri was restored

places.tagline: A red mansion with tiger trophies
places.whyGo: A red Indo-Saracenic mansion on Abul Hasnat Road with cusped arches, a double-height hall, century-old chandeliers and mirrors, and hunting trophies that gave it the name 'tiger house'. It is a family-run waqf; visitors have been welcomed by the caretaker.
places.history: Built around 1917–20 by Khan Bahadur Muhammad Fazlul Karim of the Indian Civil Service, named after the family's Haturia estate. It is linked to Dhaka's first electric lighting in 1927, and now houses a spiritual centre (Khankay-e-Alia).
places.hours: A private residence; visits at the caretaker's discretion.

photo.tips: The façade from the front lawn under the big trees.

access.note: 14 Abul Hasnat Road, Bangshal. Be respectful: it is a home and a religious space. A 360° tour is on Hidden Heritage's website.

sources.label: The Daily Star: Heritage homes of Old Dhaka (Sep 2023)

places.tagline: A zamindar's palace, now a fire station
places.whyGo: Two linked mansions with 35 rooms and tall entrances framed by Corinthian columns. Today it houses fire service quarters, so you see it from the gate, but the façade still shows how Old Dhaka's landlords lived.
places.history: Built about a century ago in the time of Ray Bahadur Satyendra Kumar Das. The road is named after his father, Revati Mohan Das. The family left at Partition in 1947 and it became vested property. It is a listed heritage site.

photo.tips: The south-facing entrance and its columns from the road.

access.note: 33 Revati Mohan Das Road, Sutrapur. A working fire station: don't block the gate.

sources.label: The Daily Star: Sutrapur Zamindar Palace (Oct 2021)
The Daily Star: Heritage homes of Old Dhaka (Sep 2023)

places.tagline: A zamindar's house turned student hostel
places.whyGo: A Neo-Classical house with three courtyards, fluted Corinthian columns, coloured-glass windows and old tiles. It is now a crowded college dormitory, so look from outside unless invited in.
places.history: Built at the end of the 19th century by zamindar Jotindra Kumar Saha. Locals call it the Khelaghar building; after 1971 it became the Shaheed Shamsul Alam dormitory of Kabi Nazrul Government College.

photo.tips: The curved front with its arches.

access.note: Shyambazar, next to Farashganj. Combine with Ruplal House and Northbrook Hall.

sources.label: Prothom Alo: Dhaka house of Zamindar Jotindra Kumar still stands (Oct 2025)

places.tagline: An ayurvedic factory from 1914, with resident monkeys
places.whyGo: Bangladesh's first ayurvedic medicine laboratory, still working on about two acres in Gendaria. A troop of monkeys lives on the grounds, one of the neighbourhood's best-known sights.
places.history: Founded in 1914 by Jogesh Chandra Ghosh and modernised in 1917. Ghosh was killed during the Liberation War in 1971. The company once made about 450 medicines and still has sales centres across the country.
places.hours: A working factory; view from outside.

photo.tips: The monkeys on the walls and trees; keep your distance and don't feed them.

access.note: Din Nath Sen Road, Gendaria.

sources.label: The Daily Star: Historic tale of Gandaria (Feb 2022)

places.tagline: A neighbourhood library in a revolutionaries' house
places.whyGo: A small community library in an old house on Din Nath Sen Road, run by the children's organisation Khelaghar Ashar. A quiet corner of Gendaria that few visitors know.
places.history: Started by Nasim Ali in his home and moved in 1946 to Ambika Charan Chakravarty's house, which sheltered anti-British revolutionaries around Partition.

photo.tips: The old house front.

access.note: Din Nath Sen Road, Gendaria, near Sadhana Aushadhalaya.

sources.label: The Daily Star: Historic tale of Gandaria (Feb 2022)

places.tagline: The school where J.C. Bose and Meghnad Saha studied
places.whyGo: One of the oldest schools in the country, at the Sadarghat crossing by the Buriganga. Physicists Jagadish Chandra Bose and Meghnad Saha and the poet Buddhadeva Bose studied here. Look in from the gate on your way between Bahadur Shah Park and the river.
places.history: Founded on 21 June 1835 as the Dhaka English Seminary. Its old main building was demolished during redevelopment despite protests by heritage activists.
places.hours: A working school; view from outside.

photo.tips: The gate and the crossing from across the road.

access.note: 1 Loyal Street, Sadarghat. A working school: keep it brief.

sources.label: The Business Standard: Activists rally against demolition of the old Collegiate School building

places.tagline: From a 1858 school to a university
places.whyGo: A crowded, lively campus beside Bahadur Shah Park whose roots go back to 1858. It shows how Old Dhaka's education grew up around the river port.
places.history: Founded in 1858 as the Dhaka Brahma School, renamed Jagannath School in 1872 after a zamindar's father, became Jagannath College in 1884, and a university in 2005.
places.hours: A working university; ask at the gate.

photo.tips: From Bahadur Shah Park looking toward the campus.

access.note: Next to Bahadur Shah Park and St Thomas Church.

places.tagline: Luchi and dal for breakfast, for almost a century
places.whyGo: A roadside breakfast place with a short menu: puffed luchi with house-seasoned dal topped with onion and coriander, and eggs finished with black salt. Light, cheap, and close to Beauty Boarding and the book lanes.
places.history: It had been running for almost a hundred years when The Business Standard wrote about it in 2020.

photo.tips: Luchi and dal on the plate, onion on top.

access.note: 47 North Brook Hall Road, Banglabazar.

sources.label: The Business Standard: 5 classic breakfast places in Dhaka (Nov 2020)

places.tagline: Rickshaw parts, rickshaw art, even whole rickshaws
places.whyGo: The street to buy rickshaw parts and the painted tin panels that decorate the back of Dhaka's rickshaws. The panels roll up to fit in a suitcase, which makes them the best souvenir in Old Dhaka.
places.history: Rickshaws and rickshaw painting in Dhaka were added to UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2023.

photo.tips: Stacks of painted panels and chrome parts in the shopfronts.

access.note: Bangshal Road, next to Kazi Alauddin Road. Budget around ৳200 for a painted panel and be ready to bargain.

sources.label: UNESCO: Rickshaws and rickshaw painting in Dhaka (inscribed 2023)

places.tagline: Tiled walls of gods on Joy Kali Temple Road
places.whyGo: A small, old temple with a mosaic floor, walls tiled with images of Hindu deities, thick square columns and arched upper walls. Few visitors find it.
places.history: Said to be nearly 400 years old, established in the Bengali year 1001 under Tulsi Narayan Ghosh and Naw Narayan Ghosh.

photo.tips: The tiled walls up close.
photo.inside: Ask first; remove shoes where asked

access.note: 24 Joy Kali Temple Road, between Thatari Bazar and Wari.

sources.label: Dhaka Tribune: 10 historic temples in Dhaka you can visit (Oct 2024)

peak: Birth anniversaries of Sri Ramakrishna, Sarada Devi and Vivekananda
places.tagline: A domed hall with symbols of six faiths
places.whyGo: A hexagonal prayer hall for about 600 people, with five entrances and a main dome ringed by six small domes, each topped with the symbol of a different religion, after Ramakrishna's teaching 'as many faiths, so many paths'.
places.history: The Dhaka centre's foundation was laid on 13 February 1916 by Swami Brahmananda and Swami Premananda. The temple was rebuilt from 2000 after 85 years of use.

photo.tips: The ring of small domes from the courtyard.

access.note: R. K. Mission Road. About a 30-minute walk from Gulistan.

sources.label: Dhaka Tribune: 10 historic temples in Dhaka you can visit (Oct 2024)

places.tagline: Where Dhaka's Rath Yatra begins
places.whyGo: The starting point of Dhaka's annual Jagannath Rath Yatra chariot procession, which ends at Dhakeshwari Temple. On ordinary days it is a working temple.
places.history: Established in 1899 under Shri Rudra Tridandi Tripurlinga Swami as the Sri Sri Radha Govinda Temple; handed to ISKCON Bangladesh in 2000.
places.hours: Not published; ask at the gate.

photo.tips: On Rath Yatra day, the chariot leaving the gate.

access.note: 79 Swamibagh Road, Gendaria.

sources.label: Dhaka Tribune: 10 historic temples in Dhaka you can visit (Oct 2024)

blurb.en: The first-timer's day: a Mughal fort, two caravanserais, the best-known biryani, the star mosque, the Nawabs' pink palace, and a boat at sunset.
blurb.bn: প্রথমবারের জন্য পুরো দিন: মোগল কেল্লা, কাটরা, নান্নার পোলাও, তারা মসজিদ, আহসান মঞ্জিল, আর সন্ধ্যায় নৌকা।

note.en: Lalbagh Fort is closed on Sunday and opens only in the afternoon on Monday. Ahsan Manzil is closed on Thursday. On Friday, skip the mosques around midday prayer.
note.bn: লালবাগ কেল্লা রবিবার বন্ধ, সোমবার খোলে দুপুরের পর। আহসান মঞ্জিল বৃহস্পতিবার বন্ধ। শুক্রবার জুমার সময় মসজিদে যাবেন না।

stops.tip: Start while it is cool. Pari Bibi's tomb sits in the middle of the lawns.
Only the southern gateway of this 1640s travellers' inn survives. Look from the lane and be polite with shopkeepers.
Look up: old arches sit above the modern shop signs.
Lunch. Order morog polao (chicken pulao) and borhani. The original is at 41 Becharam Dewri; other shops copy the name.
Go after the midday prayer. No shorts; women cover their hair; shoes off at the prayer hall.
Ring at the gate. Walk among the 18th-century Armenian gravestones.
Foreign visitors pay ৳500 (per our sources). From October to March it closes at 16:30.
Hire a small wooden boat by the hour beside the terminal. Agree the price first; life jackets are not usually provided.

name.en: Food crawl: biryani, lassi and bakarkhani

blurb.en: An afternoon into evening of Old Dhaka's classics. Share plates so you have room for the kebabs at the end.
blurb.bn: দুপুর থেকে রাত, পুরান ঢাকার চেনা স্বাদ। ভাগ করে খান, শেষে কাবাবের জায়গা রাখুন।

note.en: Most of these shops do not publish their hours, so the times are suggestions. Popular biryani can sell out; go a little early.
note.bn: বেশিরভাগ দোকানের খোলার সময় প্রকাশিত নয়, তাই সময়গুলো আনুমানিক। জনপ্রিয় বিরিয়ানি শেষ হয়ে যেতে পারে।

stops.tip: A plain Bengali lunch in the courtyard where the country's poets used to meet.
Across the road. Mutton crumb chop and milk tea.
Order the lebu sherbet (lemon) or the lassi. It is small; you may stand.
Evening batch: watch the bread slapped onto clay ovens and buy it warm.
Goat biryani on a leaf plate since 1939. The original is at 70 Kazi Alauddin Road.
Mutton chaap off the coals. Nazira Bazar turns into a food street after dark.

name.en: River and old houses at golden hour
name.bn: বিকেলের আলোয় নদী আর পুরনো বাড়ি

blurb.en: A photo walk from the kite and bangle lanes to the riverbank mansions, timed so you are on the water as the light turns gold.
blurb.bn: ঘুড়ি আর শাঁখার গলি থেকে নদীর ধারের প্রাসাদ, শেষে সূর্য ডোবার আগে নৌকায়।

note.en: Sunset is around 17:15 in winter and 18:45 in June; shift the start time to match. Shankhari Bazar is very crowded during Durga Puja.
note.bn: শীতে সূর্য ডোবে প্রায় ৫:১৫-তে, জুনে ৬:৪৫-এ; শুরুর সময় সেই মতো ঠিক করুন। দুর্গাপূজায় শাঁখারীবাজারে খুব ভিড় হয়।

stops.tip: Kite makers fill the shopfronts before Shakrain in January.
Very narrow, very deep houses, small shrines and conch-bangle cutters. Look straight down the lane.
Memorial to the sepoys hanged here in 1857. Benches and toilets.
The country's first private school. View from the street; don't photograph students.
Porters carry fresh books on their heads through the publishing lanes.
The red 1880 town hall glows in late light. Include a domed corner tower.
A crumbling columned mansion, now a spice market. Watch your footing.
From mid-river, Ahsan Manzil, Ruplal House and the launches line up in one view.

blurb.en: One morning: a Hindu temple, a Shia imambara, a Mughal mosque, the star mosque, an Armenian church and a Sikh gurdwara, then lunch on the same lane.
blurb.bn: এক সকালে মন্দির, ইমামবাড়া, মোগল আমলের মসজিদ, তারা মসজিদ, আর্মেনিয়ান গির্জা আর গুরুদুয়ারা, শেষে দুপুরের খাবার।

note.en: Dress modestly and carry a scarf. Avoid Friday midday, when the mosques are full for prayer, and Thursday at the Armenian Church, when a food programme draws crowds.
note.bn: শালীন পোশাক পরুন, একটা ওড়না বা স্কার্ফ রাখুন। শুক্রবার দুপুরে মসজিদে ভিড়, বৃহস্পতিবার আর্মেনিয়ান চার্চে ভিড় থাকে।

stops.tip: Bangladesh's largest Hindu temple, calm in the morning. Remove shoes where asked.
A white Shia imambara with a pond in front; shoot the reflection from the south bank.
Shaista Khan's 1676 mosque on the market square. Keep valuables close in the crowd.
Every surface is mosaic made from broken china. No shorts; women cover their hair.
A white 1781 church in a walled graveyard. Ring at the gate.
Linked to Guru Tegh Bahadur's stay in the 1660s. Ask at the door before going in.
Lunch on the same lane, in the poets' old courtyard.

items: Ride-hailing app.
Uber and Pathao both work in Dhaka, and drivers generally only accept cash. Ask to be dropped at Ahsan Manzil, Sadarghat or Lalbagh Fort; cars can't get into many of the lanes.
Metro Rail.
Line 6 runs from Uttara to Motijheel. From Motijheel it is about 2.5 km to Ahsan Manzil by rickshaw or CNG. Fares start at ৳20. Friday service has run in the afternoon only, so check before you go.
CNG auto-rickshaw.

The official fare is ৳40 for the first 2 km, then ৳12 per km, plus ৳2 a minute waiting. Meters are often not used, and in February 2025 the authority dropped a plan to enforce them, so agree the fare before you get in.
Walk, and take cycle rickshaws.
Distances are short but the lanes are narrow and busy. Each place card says whether a car, a rickshaw or only your feet can reach it.
Agree the fare first.

Rickshaws have no fixed fare. A common starting point is ৳15–20 per km, and short hops start at about ৳20 (Dhaka University's own campus chart runs ৳20–30). One 2025 guide puts an hour's rickshaw tour of the lanes at about ৳100. The routes and Near me show estimates.
Show the driver.
Tap “Show driver” on any place card to show its name in large Bangla. For Lalbagh Fort, drivers know it as “Lalbagh Kella”.
Leaving Sadarghat?
Walk a few hundred metres north before looking for a rickshaw. Traffic right by the port barely moves.

title.en: What to wear and how to behave

items: Cover up.
Women should cover shoulders and legs in public.
At mosques,
shorts are not allowed for anyone, and women cover their hair. Visit outside prayer times, and avoid Friday midday, when mosques are full for Jumu'ah.
Shoes off
before prayer halls and temple courtyards, where asked.
Photos.
Ask before photographing people up close, and don't photograph schoolchildren.
Carry cash in small notes.
Rickshaws, food stalls and boats take cash, and Uber drivers generally only accept cash.
Budget.
A 2025 guide estimates ৳1,000–2,000 per person for a day in Old Dhaka with food and transport, before entry tickets.
Tickets.
Each place card shows the fee we found. Ahsan Manzil charges foreign visitors ৳500.
Pick busy stalls
with people eating or queuing, and drink bottled water.
Go early for biryani.
The famous shops cook a fixed amount and can sell out.
Check the address.
Famous names are copied all over the city. The cards give the original address, for example Nanna Biryani at 41 Becharam Dewri.
Hold on to your phone and bag
in rickshaws and CNGs. Thieves often work in pairs on motorbikes or CNGs.
Crowds.
Sadarghat and Chawkbazar are packed; watch your pockets, and your step on the pontoons.
Women travellers
can face harassment. Avoid isolated lanes, and avoid riding a rickshaw alone after dark.
Boats.
Don't board an overcrowded boat; overcrowding is worst on holidays and festivals.
Rallies and strikes (hartals).
Stay away from them; they can turn violent quickly.
Air.
Pollution is high, worst in winter. A mask helps on rickshaw rides.
Late November to February
is dry and mild, about 16–26°C. It is also when the air is worst.
March to May
is the hottest stretch, up to about 35°C. July and August bring rain on roughly half the days.
Start early.
Mornings are cooler and quieter. Friday and Saturday are the weekend, and afternoons at Ahsan Manzil and Lalbagh Fort get busy.
Durga Puja, 16–21 October 2026.
Big crowds, extra security and traffic around Hindu temples, including Dhakeshwari and Shankhari Bazar.
Shakrain, mid-January.
Kites fill the sky above Old Dhaka's rooftops.
Ramadan, expected from 9 February 2027.
The Chawkbazar iftar market runs every afternoon, and opening hours change (Ahsan Manzil closes at 15:00).
Muharram.
The first ten days end with the Ashura procession from Hussaini Dalan.

festivals.when: Five days in late September or October
festivals.what: Dhaka's biggest Durga Puja is at Dhakeshwari, and Shankhari Bazar is lit up end to end. It ends with processions taking the idols to the river.
festivals.tip: Evenings are packed. Go in the late morning, keep your bag in front, and expect security checks at the temple gates.

festivals.when: 14 January, the last day of Poush
festivals.what: Families fly and fight kites from the rooftops of Shankhari Bazar, Sutrapur, Gendaria, Narinda and Lakshmibazar, and make pitha at home. After dark it turns into fireworks, lanterns and loud music.
festivals.tip: The kites are on the roofs, not in the street. Go with a local friend or ask your guesthouse; a rooftop invitation is the whole point.

festivals.when: The ninth month of the Islamic calendar, about 30 days
festivals.what: The Chawkbazar iftar market fills the square every afternoon before sunset. Opening hours change across the city; Ahsan Manzil closes at 15:00. Eid ul-Fitr follows at the end of the month.
festivals.tip: Don't eat or drink openly in the street during the day. Reach Chawkbazar by 15:00; the crush peaks just before sunset.

festivals.what: For the first ten days of Muharram, Hussaini Dalan is the centre of Old Dhaka's Shia mourning gatherings. On Ashura a procession leaves from here.
festivals.tip: This is mourning, not a festival. Watch quietly from the side, dress modestly and ask before taking photos.

festivals.when: June or July, set by the Hindu calendar
festivals.what: Jagannath's chariot is pulled from the Swamibagh temple to Dhakeshwari.
festivals.tip: Check the date with the temple a few weeks before, and expect big crowds along the route.

festivals.when: August or September, set by the Hindu calendar
festivals.what: Krishna's birthday. A procession starts at Dhakeshwari and winds through the streets of Old Dhaka. It was stopped in 1948 and has run again since 1989.
festivals.tip: The procession moves slowly through narrow lanes. Pick a spot on the route early rather than following it.

festivals.when: The new-moon night of Kartik, in October or November
festivals.what: Around a hundred pandals hang over the narrow lanes of Shankhari Bazar and Tanti Bazar, and you walk underneath them to see the goddess. Families light clay lamps at home, at temples and at crematoriums to remember their elders. The pandals stay up for five or six days before the immersion.
festivals.tip: Go after dark for the lamps. The lanes are narrow and packed, so keep children close and your bag in front.

festivals.what: Old Dhaka's night of bread and halwa. After sunset the century-old roti and halua market reopens around the Chawkbazar Shahi Mosque, and bakeries in Bangshal pile huge breads and halwa across their floors. Families share food door to door, mosques stay full, and graveyards are lit for prayers for the dead.
festivals.tip: Go after sunset; it gets busier as the night goes on. In 2026 bread sold for ৳250–300 a kilo and halwa for ৳250–350. Graveyards are for prayer, so keep your camera down there.

festivals.when: Vasant Panchami, in late January or February
festivals.what: The goddess of learning, and above all a students' festival. In Old Dhaka the puja is held in Shankhari Bazar, Tanti Bazar and at Jagannath University, with pandals in schools, temples and lanes.
festivals.tip: Mornings are for the puja itself; the afternoon is for walking between pandals. Take your shoes off at the altar and ask before photographing people praying.

name.en: Eid ul-Fitr and the Eid procession

festivals.what: Dhaka's Eid procession probably began with the Naib Nazims after they moved into Nimtali Palace in the 18th century: processions came from Churihatta, Bangshal and Nawabpur to the Eidgah. Alam Musawwir painted 39 scenes of Dhaka's Eid and Muharram processions, now in the National Museum. It was stopped in 1954, revived in 1994, and the city corporation has run a large procession since 2025.
festivals.tip: Where the procession runs changes year to year (in 2025 it was in Agargaon, not Old Dhaka), so check the news the week before. Many shops and restaurants close for a few days around Eid.

festivals.when: Every night of Ramadan, from about 2 am
festivals.what: Volunteer groups walk the lanes singing qasida, mostly in Dhaka's own Urdu, to wake people for the pre-dawn meal. The tradition goes back to the Mughals and is fading, but a few groups still sing, including one in Lalbagh.
festivals.tip: There is no schedule; you hear them rather than find them. Nazira Bazar stays open all night in Ramadan for sehri, so it makes a good base.

festivals.when: The full moon of Falgun, in March
festivals.what: Shankhari Bazar turns into a street party: powder colours, water guns, buckets from the balconies and loud music. It is Hindu in origin, but people of every faith join in and plenty come from outside Old Dhaka to take part.
festivals.tip: Wear old clothes, rub oil on your skin and hair first so the colour washes off, and keep your phone in a zip bag. If you don't want to get coloured, don't go.

festivals.what: Old Dhaka's traders clean and decorate their shops, open a new account book (hal khata) and invite customers in for sweets, a custom that goes back to the Mughals. You will see it in the old markets around Babu Bazar.
festivals.tip: If a shopkeeper offers you sweets, accept: it's a welcome, not a sales pitch. Wear something red and white to fit in.

crafts.what: Dhaka's rickshaws and their painting were added to UNESCO's list of the intangible heritage of humanity in 2023. Painters cover the back panels with flowers, birds, film stars and city scenes.
crafts.see: Only a handful of painters are left in Old Dhaka. The Daily Star found them earning about ৳250 a painting.
crafts.buy: Painted tin panels on Bangshal Road. They roll up to fit in a suitcase.

crafts.what: The Shankhari community, named after the shakha, has cut conch shell here since before the Mughals. Married Hindu women wear the white bangles.
crafts.see: Watch the cutters at work in the tiny shops of Shankhari Bazar. The shells come from Sri Lanka.
crafts.buy: Bangles and carved conch shells, from the workshops themselves.

crafts.what: Light paper kites and coated string (manja) for kite fighting are made by hand for Shakrain.
crafts.see: Tanti Bazar and Shankhari Bazar in the first two weeks of January.
crafts.buy: Kites cost little; a spool of manja is the real purchase. Handle it carefully, it cuts.

crafts.what: Layered, flaky bread baked against the walls of clay ovens, the classic Old Dhaka breakfast with tea.
crafts.see: Early morning on Agamasi Lane, when the dough is slapped onto the oven walls.
crafts.buy: By the piece or by weight, warm from the oven.

crafts.what: Mosaic made from broken china plates and tiles, pressed into plaster. The Star Mosque is covered in it.
crafts.see: Stand close to the walls of Tara Masjid: you can spot pieces of patterned teacups and plates.
crafts.buy: Not for sale; this one you only look at.

phrases.intro: Old Dhaka has its own Bangla, Dhakaiya Kutti. It is named after the rice-husking (kuta) workers who settled here around 1760, and it borrows words from Urdu and Persian. Fewer people speak it now, but older shopkeepers will light up if you try.

items.en: What did you buy at the market?

history.intro: Old Dhaka is the city the Mughals made their capital of Bengal in 1610. It lost that role a century later, lived on as a trading town under deputy governors and the East India Company, became the home of the Nawabs of Dhaka, and was the centre of the city until the new town grew north of it in the 20th century. This timeline keeps to the old city and says where each fact comes from. Dates from the 1600s are often given differently by different historians; where they disagree, both are shown.

eras.summary: A riverside settlement with a goddess temple that may have given the city its name.

events.text: The Dhakeshwari Temple is traditionally dated to the Sena king Ballal Sen. The present buildings are much later.
Raja Man Singh, Akbar's general, camps in Dhaka while fighting the Bara-Bhuiyan chiefs and builds four Shiva temples at the old Dhakeshwari site.

eras.summary: Dhaka becomes Jahangirnagar, capital of the Mughal province of Bengal, and grows rich on muslin and river trade.

events.text: Mughal general Islam Khan Chishti defeats Musa Khan, and Dhaka comes under direct Mughal control.
Islam Khan moves the capital of Bengal from Rajmahal to Dhaka and renames it Jahangirnagar, after the emperor. People keep calling it Dhaka.
The Portuguese traveller Sebastien Manrique puts the population of Dhaka and its suburbs at about 200,000.
Mir Abul Qasim, diwan of Prince Shah Shuja, builds the Bara Katra, a great travellers' inn facing the river.
Mir Jumla arrives as governor and Dhaka is the capital again. His roads and gate link the city to forts against the Magh pirates.
Subahdar Shaista Khan builds the Choto Katra.
The Dutch (1663), English (1667–68) and French (1682) open trading factories. The French site later became Ahsan Manzil.
Shaista Khan's governorship is the city's biggest building boom. The Chawk Mosque by the market square dates from 1676.
Prince Muhammad Azam, son of Aurangzeb, begins the fort at Lalbagh. He is recalled before it is finished.
Shaista Khan's daughter Pari Bibi dies and work on Lalbagh Fort stops. Her tomb stands at its centre.
Dhaka is the world centre of muslin, a cotton cloth so fine that the finest grades were reserved for the Mughal court.
Kartalab Khan (Murshid Quli Khan, then Dhaka's diwan) builds the Begum Bazar mosque, and Khan Mohammad Mridha raises his mosque on a high platform.
The capital of Bengal moves to Murshidabad, and Dhaka begins a long decline.

eras.summary: Dhaka is ruled by deputy governors (Naib Nazims), then by the East India Company. Armenian and European merchants settle, and the muslin trade collapses.

events.text: Naib Nazim Mirza Lutfullah builds the Chowk Bazaar, still the old city's market square.
Rice-husking workers settle in Dhaka. Their speech becomes Dhakaiya Kutti, the old city's own Bangla.
The East India Company takes over Bengal's revenue. The Naib Nazims move into a new palace at Nimtali; its gateway survives.
The Armenian community builds the Church of the Holy Resurrection in Armanitola.
The Company abolishes the Nizamat and takes full control. The city is now written "Dacca".
British observers already call Dhaka muslin extinct: British tariffs and cheap Lancashire cotton have ruined the weavers.
The population falls from about 200,000 to 51,636.
St Thomas Church is built near the river and consecrated.
Armenian merchant Stephen Aratoon builds the mansion that becomes Ruplal House.
The Dhaka English Seminary opens; it is now Dhaka Collegiate School.
The last Naib Nazim dies and the office ends. The head of the Khwaja family estate becomes known as the Nawab of Dhaka.
Nicholas Pogose, an Armenian, founds Pogose School, the country's first private school.

eras.summary: The Nawabs build Ahsan Manzil, the city gets a municipality, a railway and a riverfront promenade, and in 1905 Dhaka briefly becomes a provincial capital.

events.text: During the sepoy uprising, British troops and sepoys clash at Lalbagh Fort on 22 November. Captured sepoys are hanged at Antaghar, today's Bahadur Shah Park.
The Dhaka Brahma School opens; it grows into Jagannath University.
Nawab Abdul Ghani builds Ahsan Manzil on the river.
The Dacca Municipality is founded, and the Buckland Bund promenade is built along the Sadarghat waterfront.
The first census counts 69,212 people.
Northbrook Hall opens as the town hall.
The railway reaches Dhaka from Narayanganj, cutting through the Nimtali–Fulbaria area.
A tornado wrecks Ahsan Manzil except its Rangmahal.
A great earthquake damages Ahsan Manzil, the Armenian Church tower, Ruplal House and Hussaini Dalan.
Dhaka becomes capital of Eastern Bengal and Assam; the partition is annulled in 1911. The Nawab of Dhaka, Salimullah, helps found the Muslim League in Dhaka in 1906.
Jogesh Chandra Ghosh founds Sadhana Aushadhalaya, an ayurvedic factory in Gendaria.
Beauty Lassi (1922) and Haji Biryani (1939) open, two of the old city's longest-running food shops.
Partition. Dhaka becomes capital of East Bengal in Pakistan. Some Hindu families leave, among them the owners of the Sutrapur Zamindar Bari, and Dhakeshwari's original idol goes to Kolkata.

eras.summary: Old Dhaka becomes the base of East Pakistan's publishers and the birthplace of the Awami League, and is attacked in 1971.

events.text: The Awami Muslim League, later the Awami League, is founded at Rose Garden Palace on 23 June.
Beauty Boarding opens and becomes a meeting place for writers and artists.
The Eid procession, an old Dhaka tradition, is stopped by the district magistrate. It does not return for 42 years.
Victoria Park is renamed Bahadur Shah Park, after the last Mughal emperor.
The Pakistan army attacks Shankhari Bazar, killing Hindu residents and burning houses. Survivors flee across the river. A memorial stands at the east end of the road.
Jogesh Chandra Ghosh, founder of Sadhana Aushadhalaya, is killed during the war. Dhaka is liberated on 16 December and becomes the capital of Bangladesh.

eras.summary: The old city restores its palaces, loses some of its heritage, lives through deadly fires, and gets its crafts and festivals recognised again.

events.text: Ahsan Manzil is restored and opens as a branch of the National Museum.
The Eid procession is revived, with young people from about 30 neighbourhoods.
Dhakeshwari is declared the National Temple.
Jagannath College becomes Jagannath University.
The Asiatic Society restores the Nimtali gateway.
A fire spreading from a chemical store in Nimtali kills at least 124 people.
Dhaka City Corporation splits in two; Old Dhaka falls under Dhaka South.
The government launches a project to bring back Dhaka muslin.
A chemical vapour explosion at Churihatta, Chawkbazar, starts a fire that kills 71 people.
Part of the Bara Katra is demolished amid ownership disputes. The Padma Bridge opens, and the Sadarghat launch fleet starts to shrink.
UNESCO lists Dhaka's rickshaws and rickshaw painting as intangible cultural heritage.
Dhaka's city corporation stages a large Eid procession again.
Restoration of Northbrook Hall is largely complete by May.
